title: Riyadh schools shift to remote learning as Houthis claim downed drone
body: Neither development is a direct market mover on its own, but together they add to the sense of escalating regional risk that oil markets have been pricing through the Iran conflict. A week-long, unexplained shift to remote schooling in a capital city is the kind of precautionary civil measure that tends to get read as a signal of heightened security concern, even without official confirmation of a specific threat, and it sits alongside this weekend's other Gulf headlines, including the reported Hormuz missile incident. The Houthi claim of downing a Saudi drone, if accurate, points to continued direct military friction between Yemen's Houthi forces and Saudi Arabia, reinforcing the theme of Saudi Arabia being drawn deeper into the wider conflict. Oil remains the primary channel through which this kind of headline risk reaches markets, with any further escalation involving Saudi territory or Saudi oil infrastructure the key trigger to watch for a larger price reaction. -- Riyadh's schools are going remote for a week with no explanation offered, landing the same weekend Yemen's Houthi forces say they downed a Saudi drone, and neither looks like coincidence given the state of the wider conflict. Summary: Gulf News reports Saudi authorities have instructed all schools in Riyadh to suspend in-person classes for one week and move entirely to distance learning via the Madrasati platform.

title: Apollo's Slok warns AI agents could trigger a bank run ("agentic bank run" is still a run...)
body: This is a scenario warning from Apollo's chief economist, not a live event, so the direct market impact today is limited, but the underlying rate gap it highlights is real and already priced into deposit flows. The chart Slok cites shows fintech and neobank products paying between 3.3 percent and 5 percent, against FDIC national averages of just 0.4 percent on savings accounts and 0.1 percent on checking accounts, a spread of up to roughly 4.9 percentage points at the top end. If agentic AI tools accelerate that existing deposit migration by automating it at scale, the risk Slok flags is a faster erosion of banks' cheap funding base, which would matter for bank net interest margins, lending capacity and, in a stress scenario, funding stability more broadly. For now this sits as a forward-looking risk to watch rather than a confirmed trend, and it is worth monitoring regional bank commentary and deposit data for early signs of the dynamic Slok describes. --- Speaking of banks... US bank failures in 2026, 6 now. California seizes Nano Banc. --- Slok's warning is less about any single bank and more about what happens to the entire system if millions of households let an AI agent chase the best rate automatically, all at once. Summary: Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok has raised the prospect of an "agentic bank run", in which AI assistants automatically move household cash into higher-yielding accounts.

title: US bank failures in 2026, 6 now. California seizes Nano Banc.
body: This reads as a governance and supervision story more than a systemic one: DFPI's own account points to years of board turmoil, executive self-dealing and repeated non-compliance with enforcement orders, rather than a sudden, broad-based credit event. At roughly $690 million in total assets, Nano Banc is too small to move markets directly, but the case adds to a running theme of regulators tightening scrutiny of governance and capital adequacy at smaller banks, particularly notable given DFPI's separate, recent public opposition to a federal proposal to loosen oversight of bank management. Depositors, including holders of uninsured deposits, are being made whole through Sunwest Bank's assumption of the book, limiting any contagion risk from this specific case. The more durable macro takeaway is the reminder that deposit insurance fund costs and heightened supervisory attention on weaker regional lenders remain live, background considerations for bank-sector positioning even when an individual failure is idiosyncratic. --- Eyes will be on these ahead of US markts repopening at 6pm Sudney, US Eastern time: China may let Alibaba, ByteDance buy new Nvidia chips, The Information reports Iran holds line on diplomacy as Hormuz missile strike raises risk before open --- A bank failure is never a good sign, and Nano Banc's seizure looks less like a sudden shock and more like the end point of years of governance failures that regulators tried, and failed, to fix.

title: China may let Alibaba, ByteDance buy new Nvidia chips, The Information reports
body: Any easing in China's stance on Nvidia purchases would be read as a modest positive for Nvidia and the broader AI supply chain, though the report is unverified and the chip in question, the RTX Pro 5500, is a professional workstation part rather than Nvidia's flagship AI accelerator, limiting the scale of the read-through. The first market reaction will likely show up not in cash equities, which are closed, but in US index futures: CME Globex reopens for the new week at 6pm US Eastern time (2200 GMT), and that reopen is typically the first point where a headline like this, alongside the Hormuz and Iran developments, gets priced into equity index futures ahead of Monday's cash session. Confirmation or denial of the report, either from Beijing or from Nvidia, would be the key catalyst for a bigger move either way. --- China may be preparing to let Alibaba and ByteDance buy Nvidia's newest high-end chip, an unverified report says, in a move some industry executives think could sidestep existing US export rules. Summary: The Information reports, citing two people familiar with the matter, that China's government has signalled it could allow domestic firms including ByteDance and Alibaba to buy Nvidia's RTX Pro 5500 chip. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has reportedly asked companies including ByteDance and Alibaba to detail their purchase plans for the chip, including quantities and intended use.

title: Iran holds line on diplomacy as Hormuz missile strike raises risk before open
body: Oil carries the risk premium into the new week. A reported Iranian cruise missile strike on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, still unconfirmed by independent sources, is the kind of headline that can gap crude higher at the open regardless of how it is ultimately verified, given the volume of global supply that transits the chokepoint. Iran's insistence that any reopening of Hormuz stays contingent on its own conditions, combined with Trump's rejection of Tehran's offer, points to a blockade and shipping disruption that persist rather than ease this week. Saudi Arabia's deepening exposure, with Houthi advances now threatening its oil exports through the Red Sea, adds a second, broadening front to the supply risk. Equity and FX markets are more likely to take direction from oil's reaction than from the diplomatic back and forth itself, with any escalation in the Gulf also supportive of the US dollar and other traditional havens. --- Markets open the week with the Hormuz standoff unresolved, diplomacy stalled but not dead, and an unverified Iranian claim of a fresh missile strike in the Strait adding an immediate layer of headline risk to oil. title: Waltz calls Iran's Hormuz proposal a cynical bid for upfront concessions
body: The dispute over what exactly Iran offered, and why the US rejected it, matters more for the diplomatic timeline than for any single price move today, but it keeps the core oil market risk unresolved heading into the week: neither side is describing a deal as imminent. Waltz's framing of Iran's proposal as front-loaded and "cynical" suggests the US side sees little near-term prospect of a negotiated Hormuz reopening, which argues for continued elevated risk premium in oil rather than a fade. The Wall Street Journal's report that Trump has told aides he expects to resume strikes after the midterms, while described by Waltz only as "anonymous reporting" rather than confirmed or denied, adds a specific, dated escalation risk to watch for later in the year if verified. Iran's insistence, through both Araghchi and Pezeshkian, that any reopening remains conditional on frozen assets and eased sanctions keeps the standoff structurally unchanged, reinforcing oil and safe-haven positioning as the most direct channels for this story to reach markets this week.

title: Bessent urges Fed to keep an open mind on rates, citing AI productivity
body: Bessent's comments are best read as the Treasury Secretary's own advocacy for a looser Fed reaction function rather than a signal of imminent policy change, but the framing matters for rate expectations given his direct line to a Fed chair the administration itself selected. Explicitly invoking the Greenspan late-1990s precedent, where the Fed tolerated stronger growth on productivity grounds, suggests the administration wants markets to expect the Fed to look through near-term inflation prints if AI-driven productivity gains can be credited for offsetting them. That framing runs alongside a genuine near-term inflation complication: Iran-war-linked fuel costs remain elevated and are already showing up in core CPI and bond yields, and Bessent's own comments acknowledge those costs are weighing on voters. His remarks on Iranian oil deliveries to China potentially ending within two weeks are also relevant for oil markets, since a further tightening of Iran's remaining export outlets would reinforce upside price risk at exactly the same time the broader Hormuz standoff remains unresolved. Bessent wants the Fed to treat today's AI boom like Greenspan treated the 1990s internet boom, waving through faster growth even as Iran-linked fuel costs keep showing up in the inflation data.
